  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:
<br class="ltx_break">A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Diffusion models generate high-quality samples but can also memorize training data, raising serious privacy concerns. Understanding the mechanisms governing when memorization versus generalization occurs remains an active area of research. In particular, it is unclear where along the noise schedule memorization is induced, how data geometry influences it, and how phenomena at different noise scales interact. We introduce a geometric framework that partitions the noise schedule into three regimes based on the coverage properties of training data by Gaussian shells and the concentration behavior of the posterior, which we argue are two fundamental objects governing memorization and generalization in diffusion models. This perspective reveals that memorization risk is highly non-uniform across noise levels. We further identify a danger zone at medium noise levels where memorization is most pronounced. In contrast, both the small and large noise regimes resist memorization, but through fundamentally different mechanisms: small noise avoids memorization due to limited training coverage, while large noise exhibits low posterior concentration and admits a provably near linear Gaussian denoising behavior.
For the medium noise regime, we identify geometric conditions through which we propose a geometry-informed targeted intervention that mitigates memorization.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Diffusion models have achieved remarkable success in generative modeling, producing high-quality images but sometimes memorizing the training data, raising serious privacy and copyright concerns <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>.
This memorization risk is inherent to the training objective, as it admits a unique global minimum, namely the <em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">empirical optimal</em> solution, which can only generate the training data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>.
Consequently, it is both theoretically interesting and practically important to understand how and when a learned model can deviate from the empirical optimal to generalize beyond its training data.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Some recent works have analyzed this question. In particular, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite> argues that the stochastic nature of diffusion model training helps prevent fitting the empirical optimal denoiser, and thus promotes generalization.
Later, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> contests this view, showing that for a large range of training times the regression target is essentially unique while model still generalizes.
Recently, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> point out that supervised training in diffusion models is limited to small regions which fails to cover most parts of the inference trajectory, and argues that the generalization behavior of the model stems from extrapolation.</p>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Our work.</h5>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A key aspect to understand when models <em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">generalize</em> is to understand when they <em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">memorize</em>, which we focus on in this paper.
To this end, we distinguish between <em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">trajectory-level memorization</em>, which concerns whether full sampling trajectories collapse to the training set, and <em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">per-noise-level memorization</em>, which characterizes memorizing denoiser behavior at a fixed noise scale.
Empirically, we find that models exhibiting strong trajectory-level memorization may nonetheless behave benignly at many individual noise levels, indicating that memorization is not induced uniformly across the noise schedule (see <a href="#S3" title="3 Empirical Investigation of Memorization ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> for more details).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This observation motivates our central question: <em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">At which noise levels is memorization formed, and what geometric mechanisms govern its emergence?</em></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To address these questions, we analyze diffusion training through a geometric lens based on two quantities: <em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">posterior weight concentration</em> and <em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Gaussian shell coverage</em> of the training data. This perspective naturally partitions the noise schedule into three regimes. At both small and large noise levels, the training lies on “calm ends” that are resistant to memorization, but for fundamentally different reasons: in the small noise regime, memorization is suppressed due to limited training coverage, while in the large noise regime due to weak posterior concentration and effectively linear denoising behavior. In contrast, a “danger zone” emerges at intermediate noise level – the “wild middle” – where these two effects align and memorization risk peaks sharply. Crucially, memorization formed in this regime can propagate along the inference trajectory and persist into the small noise stage, leading the model to memorize even when both ends of the schedule remain benign. This observation suggests that, to avoid memorization, it is most effective to control the behavior of diffusion models specifically within this intermediate “danger zone”. By analyzing how coverage and posterior concentration interact, we can predict the location of this danger zone directly from the dataset. Experiments in Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Targeted Noise Region Undertraining ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> confirm this picture and show that selectively undertraining the intermediate regime can substantially mitigate memorization while preserving generation quality.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">More related work.</h5>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Several explanations have been proposed for diffusion model generalization. Notably, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite> shows that models in the generalization regime exhibit closeness to a Gaussian linear model, suggesting an inductive bias toward learning the covariance structure.
Neural networks also exhibit spectral bias <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, which may influence what diffusion models learn. Other factors known to promote generalization include early stopping before memorization occurs, limiting model capacity relative to dataset size <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>, increasing the amount of training data as the scaling behavior for generalization and memorization differ in terms of the number of data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, and conditional training with auxiliary noise classes to provide distributional contrast <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> denote a data distribution on <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>. Let <math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{X}\sim p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝑿</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{X}\sim p</annotation></semantics></math> denote a random variable following <math id="S2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝒁</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})</annotation></semantics></math> a standard Gaussian random variable independent of <math id="S2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝑿</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{X}</annotation></semantics></math>. For the training and sampling of diffusion models, we mostly follow the description given in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Training.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In diffusion models, one of the central tasks is to denoise a noisy observation <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{X}_{\sigma}=\bm{X}+\sigma\bm{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝑿</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒁</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{X}_{\sigma}=\bm{X}+\sigma\bm{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> for various noise levels <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> in order to obtain <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝑿</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{X}</annotation></semantics></math>. In particular, one popular diffusion training loss is defined as</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{X}\sim p\\
\bm{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})\\
\sigma\sim\lambda\end{subarray}}\left\|m^{\theta}_{\sigma}(\bm{X}_{\sigma})-\bm{X}\right\|^{2}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mtable rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>𝑿</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>𝒁</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑿</mi></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{X}\sim p\\
\bm{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})\\
\sigma\sim\lambda\end{subarray}}\left\|m^{\theta}_{\sigma}(\bm{X}_{\sigma})-\bm{X}\right\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> denotes certain distribution on some chosen <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\sigma_{\min},\sigma_{\max}]\subset(0,\infty)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>⊂</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\sigma_{\min},\sigma_{\max}]\subset(0,\infty)</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}^{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}^{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> is a neural network parameterized by <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> that aims to approximate the <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">(optimal) denoiser</em> <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math> that we will introduce below. We refer to <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}^{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}^{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> as a <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">trained denoiser</em> in what follows.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Optimal solution.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The above loss admits a unique global minimum given by the posterior mean which we call the <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">optimal denoiser</em>:
<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}(x):=\mathbb{E}[\bm{X}\mid\bm{X}_{\sigma}=x]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>𝑿</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}(x):=\mathbb{E}[\bm{X}\mid\bm{X}_{\sigma}=x]</annotation></semantics></math>.
In practice, a model is trained with finite samples <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math> assumed to be drawn i.i.d. from some data distribution <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>. In this case, the expectation over <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{X}\sim p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝑿</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{X}\sim p</annotation></semantics></math> in the training loss <a href="#S2.E1" title="In Training. ‣ 2 Background ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eqn.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> can be replaced by <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{X}\sim p_{\mathcal{D}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝑿</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{X}\sim p_{\mathcal{D}}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\mathcal{D}}:=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{x_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>δ</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\mathcal{D}}:=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{x_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the resulting optimal denoiser, which we now call the <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">empirical optimal denoiser</em>, has a closed form given by</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}(x,\sigma)x_{i}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}(x,\sigma)x_{i}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{i}(x,\sigma)=\mathbb{P}(\bm{X}=x_{i}\mid\bm{X}_{\sigma}=x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ℙ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝑿</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{i}(x,\sigma)=\mathbb{P}(\bm{X}=x_{i}\mid\bm{X}_{\sigma}=x)</annotation></semantics></math> is called the <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">posterior weight</em> on <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> at the noise level <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> and is given by</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{i}(x,\sigma)=\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{\|x-x_{i}\|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp\left(-\frac{\|x-x_{j}\|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{i}(x,\sigma)=\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{\|x-x_{i}\|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp\left(-\frac{\|x-x_{j}\|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Sampling.</span> After training, one samples <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})</annotation></semantics></math> and lets <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{\sigma_{\max}}=\sigma_{\max}z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{\sigma_{\max}}=\sigma_{\max}z</annotation></semantics></math> for some large <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math>. New samples are generated by solving the following ODE:</p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{dx_{\sigma}}/{d\sigma}=-({m_{\sigma}^{\theta}(x_{\sigma})-x_{\sigma}})/{\sigma}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>σ</mi><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{dx_{\sigma}}/{d\sigma}=-({m_{\sigma}^{\theta}(x_{\sigma})-x_{\sigma}})/{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">from <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\min}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\min}</annotation></semantics></math>. For any <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma\in[\sigma_{\min},\sigma_{\max}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma\in[\sigma_{\min},\sigma_{\max}]</annotation></semantics></math>, we denote by <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Psi^{\theta}_{\sigma}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><mi>σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Psi^{\theta}_{\sigma}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> the flow map induced by the denoiser <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}^{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}^{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, which maps <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{\sigma_{\max}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{\sigma_{\max}}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{\sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math> by solving the ODE above.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17846v1/plot1_mse_to_clean.svg" id="S2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/214;" width="452" height="214"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S2.F1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">MSE to Clean Image.<span id="S2.F1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Comparison of denoising quality across noise levels. Solid lines: training data; dotted lines: test data. </span>EDM-1K<span id="S2.F1.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> shows a generalization gap in the mid-<math id="S2.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> region.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Empirical Investigation of Memorization</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To understand where and how memorization emerges during diffusion model training, we begin with an empirical investigation that motivates our subsequent geometric framework. By comparing models with different memorization behaviors across the noise schedule, we find the intermediate noise level is the most susceptible to memorization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We start by comparing trained denoisers and the empirical optimal denoiser on the CIFAR-10 dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>. We adopt the EDM from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> to model <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}^{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}^{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> and consider three denoisers: a full-data EDM denoiser trained on 50k images (<span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EDM-50K</span>),
an EDM denoiser trained on only 1k images (<span id="S3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EDM-1K</span>)<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          Training on 1k CIFAR-10 images is known to lead to memorization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>. We also validate this in <a href="#S3.T1" title="In Trajectory-Level memorization. ‣ 3 Empirical Investigation of Memorization ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. The 1k data is the first 1k in CIFAR-10 which is randomly indexed.</span></span></span>,
and the empirical optimal denoiser under the same 1k training images (<span id="S3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EMP-1K</span>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">One straightforward way to compare the three models is to evaluate their denoising losses via <a href="#S2.E1" title="In Training. ‣ 2 Background ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eqn.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. For a fixed noise level <math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, this objective reduces to the denoising mean squared error (MSE). We therefore evaluate the fixed-<math id="S3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> denoising MSE of the three models over <math id="S3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma\in[0.002,80]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0.002</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>80</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma\in[0.002,80]</annotation></semantics></math> on both training and test data from CIFAR-10:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{MSE}_{\sigma}(p_{\bullet}):=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{X}\sim p_{\bullet}\\
\bm{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})\end{subarray}}\left\|m_{\sigma}^{\bullet}(\bm{X}_{\sigma})-\bm{X}\right\|^{2}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>MSE</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mo>∙</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mtable rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>𝑿</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mo>∙</mo></msub></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>𝒁</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mo>∙</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>𝑿</mi></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{MSE}_{\sigma}(p_{\bullet}):=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{X}\sim p_{\bullet}\\
\bm{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})\end{subarray}}\left\|m_{\sigma}^{\bullet}(\bm{X}_{\sigma})-\bm{X}\right\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}^{\bullet}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mo>∙</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}^{\bullet}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes either a trained or an optimal denoiser and <math id="S3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\bullet}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mo>∙</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\bullet}</annotation></semantics></math> is either the training distribution <math id="S3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\mathcal{D}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\mathcal{D}}</annotation></semantics></math> or the test distribution <math id="S3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\mathcal{T}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\mathcal{T}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Intuitively, <math id="S3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{MSE}_{\sigma}(p_{\mathcal{D}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>MSE</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{MSE}_{\sigma}(p_{\mathcal{D}})</annotation></semantics></math> measures how well a model can recover a training image from its noisy version at noise level <math id="S3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, while <math id="S3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{MSE}_{\sigma}(p_{\mathcal{T}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>MSE</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{MSE}_{\sigma}(p_{\mathcal{T}})</annotation></semantics></math> measures the corresponding performance on unseen test images. Taken together, these two quantities provide a coarse diagnostic of generalization behavior across noise scales: a small train–test gap suggests similar behavior on training and test data, whereas a large gap indicates degradation on test samples and may signal memorization. We emphasize, however, that train–test MSE alone is not a definitive measure of memorization, but serves here as a useful summary statistic.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17846v1/per_noise_level_memorization_rate.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/203;" width="452" height="203" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Per-Noise-Level Memorization Rate.<span id="S3.F2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Fraction of denoised test images classified as memorized at each noise level.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The results are shown in <a href="#S2.F1" title="In Optimal solution. ‣ 2 Background ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Interestingly, we observe three distinct noise regions in which the three models exhibit qualitatively different behavior. At this stage, this partition is purely observational; in subsequent sections, we provide a geometric characterization that explains the emergence of these large-, intermediate-, and small noise regimes.</p>
<ol id="S3.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At large <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> (i.e., large noise), all three denoisers behave similarly on both train and test. We will later explain in <a href="#S4.SS2.SSS2" title="4.2.2 Large Noise Regime ‣ 4.2 Characterization of the Noise Regimes ‣ 4 Geometric Interpretation of Noise Regimes ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2.2</span></a> that this is due to the fact that high noise denoising is dominated by coarse statistics.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At middle <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EMP-1K</span> sharply diverges from <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EDM-50K</span>, achieving near-zero training error but large test error due to its nearest-neighbor nature, while <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EDM-50K</span> continues to generalize well.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Interestingly, at small <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, although <span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EDM-1K</span> generates training data during sampling, it differs from <span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EMP-1K</span> (the empirical optimal denoiser) in its per <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>-level denoising behavior on test data.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">This three-regime pattern motivates a closer examination of memorization for the three denoisers. In particular, instead of only considering the classic notion of memorization, we should also consider memorization risk <span id="S3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">at each noise level</span>. While the MSE gap between train and test data may be a good metric for generalization, it is not directly capturing memorization. To resolve this issue, we propose the following metrics for evaluating memorization.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Trajectory-Level memorization.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For a denoiser <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m^{\bullet}_{\sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mo>∙</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m^{\bullet}_{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math> with noise schedule <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma\in[\sigma_{\text{min}},\sigma_{\text{max}}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mtext>min</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mtext>max</mtext></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma\in[\sigma_{\text{min}},\sigma_{\text{max}}]</annotation></semantics></math>, let <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Psi^{\bullet}_{\sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><mi>σ</mi><mo>∙</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Psi^{\bullet}_{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math> be the resulting flow map given by solving <a href="#S2.E4" title="In Optimal solution. ‣ 2 Background ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eqn.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. Intuitively, the denoiser <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m^{\bullet}_{\sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mo>∙</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m^{\bullet}_{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math> is said to have memorized the data set <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> if its generated samples through the flow map are close to one of the data points in <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>. While there could be many ways of quantifying this intuition, we adopt the idea from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>, in which they proposed to classify a generated sample as memorized if it is significantly closer to its nearest training neighbor than to the second nearest. Formally, we say <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{m^{\bullet}_{\sigma}\}_{\sigma\in[\sigma_{\min},\sigma_{\max}]}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mo>∙</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{m^{\bullet}_{\sigma}\}_{\sigma\in[\sigma_{\min},\sigma_{\max}]}</annotation></semantics></math> is memorizing if for a large portion of noise samples <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{Z}\sim N(0,I_{d})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝒁</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{Z}\sim N(0,I_{d})</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{1\mathrm{NN}}(\Psi^{\bullet}_{\sigma_{\text{min}}}(\sigma_{\text{max}}\bm{Z}))&lt;d_{2\mathrm{NN}}(\Psi^{\bullet}_{\sigma_{\text{min}}}(\sigma_{\text{max}}\bm{Z})/3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><msub><mi>σ</mi><mtext>min</mtext></msub><mo>∙</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mtext>max</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒁</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mi><msub><mi>σ</mi><mtext>min</mtext></msub><mo>∙</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mtext>max</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒁</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">CLOSE</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{1\mathrm{NN}}(\Psi^{\bullet}_{\sigma_{\text{min}}}(\sigma_{\text{max}}\bm{Z}))&lt;d_{2\mathrm{NN}}(\Psi^{\bullet}_{\sigma_{\text{min}}}(\sigma_{\text{max}}\bm{Z})/3</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{K\mathrm{NN}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>NN</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{K\mathrm{NN}}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the distance to the <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>th nearest point in <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>. In particular, we compute the ratio of samples satisfying this condition to quantify the trajectory-level memorization rate.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S3.T1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Memorization Rates in Denoiser Swapping.<span id="S3.T1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Memorization measured as fraction of 256 samples where <math id="S3.T1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{1\mathrm{NN}}&lt;d_{2\mathrm{NN}}/3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow></msub><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{1\mathrm{NN}}&lt;d_{2\mathrm{NN}}/3</annotation></semantics></math>. Swapping in medium region flips behavior. </span></span></figcaption>
<table id="S3.T1.6" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S3.T1.6.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S3.T1.6.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T1.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Condition</span></th>
<td id="S3.T1.6.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T1.6.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Noise Range (<math id="S3.T1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>)</span></td>
