<td id="S4.SS2.p3.1.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.5.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">High</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">While informal this description may serve as a guiding principal for classifying training dynamics across a full noise schedule. Precise estimation of noise ranges requires further work, but our <a href="#S4.Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 4.2. ‣ 4.1 Key Players for Per-Noise-Level Memorizations ‣ 4 Geometric Interpretation of Noise Regimes ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a> and <a href="#S4.Thmtheorem8" title="Theorem 4.8. ‣ 4.1 Key Players for Per-Noise-Level Memorizations ‣ 4 Geometric Interpretation of Noise Regimes ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.8</span></a> serve as a starting point. In what follows, we provide rationales for this characterization and further analysis within each regime.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.1 </span>Small Noise Regime</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The small noise (small <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>) regime is characterized by high posterior weight and low coverage.
This is where the empirical optimal denoiser behaves almost like a nearest neighbor map. If a trained model well approximates the empirical optimal one, it will absolutely produce memorized training data and hence it is natural to suggest mitigation for memorization in this region <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>. However, although the empirical optimal denoiser exhibits strong memorization behavior (which is almost locally constant), the trained denoiser is unlikely to fit the empirical optimal denoiser since the supervision region during training, described by shell coverage, is very limited.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We have empirically observed in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Empirical Investigation of Memorization ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> that the small noise regime is quite safe from memorization risk in per-noise-level: while the empirical optimal denoiser exhibits nearly 100% memorization for <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma&lt;0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma&lt;0.3</annotation></semantics></math>, the learned model (<span id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EDM-1K</span>) shows minimal memorization in this regime. We also validate in the swapping experiment in <a href="#S3.T1" title="In Trajectory-Level memorization. ‣ 3 Empirical Investigation of Memorization ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> that the small noise regime in a trained diffusion model does not contribute to memorization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Within the small noise regime, when <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is small enough (e.g., <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;0.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;0.2</annotation></semantics></math> for the CIFAR-10), all Gaussian shells around data points will be disjoint. In this setting, we have the following description of the optimal solution to the training objective. See Theorem <a href="#A2.Thmtheorem6" title="Theorem B.6. ‣ B.2 Proof of ‣ Appendix B Gaussian Shell and Coverage ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.6</span></a> for the complete statement and proof.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.Thmtheorem9" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S4.Thmtheorem9.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 4.9</span></span><span id="S4.Thmtheorem9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Informal theorem)<span id="S4.Thmtheorem9.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S4.Thmtheorem9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.Thmtheorem9.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.Thmtheorem9.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Suppose the training is only restricted to the union of shells <math id="S4.Thmtheorem9.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bigcup_{i=1}^{N}S_{\sigma}({x_{i}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo>⋃</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bigcup_{i=1}^{N}S_{\sigma}({x_{i}})</annotation></semantics></math>, which are also pairwise disjoint for small <math id="S4.Thmtheorem9.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>. Then, there are infinitely many global minimizers of the denoising objective sending <math id="S4.Thmtheorem9.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{\sigma}({x_{i}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\sigma}({x_{i}})</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.Thmtheorem9.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S4.Thmtheorem9.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i=1,\ldots,N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i=1,\ldots,N</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In the small-<math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> regime, training supervision is concentrated within the small region consisting of the union of Gaussian shells. Then by Theorem <a href="#S4.Thmtheorem9" title="Theorem 4.9 (Informal theorem). ‣ 4.2.1 Small Noise Regime ‣ 4.2 Characterization of the Noise Regimes ‣ 4 Geometric Interpretation of Noise Regimes ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.9</span></a>, the training objective alone does not constrain the denoiser outside this small region, so extrapolation behavior is largely determined by the model’s inductive bias.
In one dimension, shallow network denoisers have been shown to interpolate the data with piecewise linear behavior <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>.
In high dimensional and deep network settings, this behavior may not hold. Below we try to provide some evidence that certain locality inductive bias will appear for image datasets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">For an image data such as CIFAR-10, we hypothesize that the locality increases when <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> decreases: each output pixel depends mainly on a local patch. The task therefore reduces to patch denoising in a much lower-dimensional subspace, where the effective training data, the extracted patches, are plentiful, making the problem easier. This aligns with empirical findings in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>: trained neural denoisers exhibit shrinking receptive fields as the noise level decreases.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite> finds the optimal denoiser under locality bias and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> connects the localization to the data statistics.
However, it was not clear what affects the spatial decay rate of the sensitivity. To study this analytically, we model the data as a Gaussian with circulant covariance—a natural idealization, since natural images exhibit approximately translation-invariant second-order statistics and stationary Gaussian models are a standard tool in their analysis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>. We propose the following theorem; formal statements and proofs are in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Sensitivity Localization ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.Thmtheorem10" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S4.Thmtheorem10.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 4.10</span></span><span id="S4.Thmtheorem10.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Informal theorem)<span id="S4.Thmtheorem10.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S4.Thmtheorem10.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.Thmtheorem10.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.Thmtheorem10.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For a cyclic stationary Gaussian data distribution, at any noise level <math id="S4.Thmtheorem10.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, the sensitivity between two pixels is bounded by <math id="S4.Thmtheorem10.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{T_{\sigma}}{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mi>m</mi></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{T_{\sigma}}{m}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.Thmtheorem10.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> is their wrap-around distance and <math id="S4.Thmtheorem10.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math> is a constant depending only on the data spectrum and <math id="S4.Thmtheorem10.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>. A more concentrated spectrum leads to faster decay of the sensitivity.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.2 </span>Large Noise Regime</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We characterize the large noise regime by low posterior weight and high coverage. The latter implies that the model <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}^{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}^{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> can learn the empirical optimal on a region that covers most of the mass of <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math>, where inference takes place. In this regime, the empirical optimal denoiser does not exhibit per-noise-level memorization behavior, and hence even if the trained denoiser closely approximates the empirical optimal denoiser, per-noise-level memorization risk remains low.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In fact, we can provide some more refined description of the empirical optimal denoiser within this regime.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">It is known that when <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is large, the denoiser <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math> will be close to the mean <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> of the data distribution <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>. Empirically, it has also been observed that <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math> behaves like a linear map when <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is large <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>. In what follows, we reconcile these two observations by establishing the limiting behavior of <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math> when <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is large.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math> denote the covariance of <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>, and recall that <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> is the mean of <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>. Consider now the Gaussian distribution <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> that matches the mean and covariance of <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>. The denoiser <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}^{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mi>G</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}^{G}</annotation></semantics></math> of this Gaussian distribution is linear and has the closed form <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>:</p>
<table id="S4.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}^{G}(x)=\mu+\Sigma(\Sigma+\sigma^{2}I)^{-1}(x-\mu)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mi>G</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}^{G}(x)=\mu+\Sigma(\Sigma+\sigma^{2}I)^{-1}(x-\mu).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p4.2" class="ltx_p">Note that when <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is large, the linear term will be small and hence <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}^{G}\approx\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mi>G</mi></msubsup><mo>≈</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}^{G}\approx\mu</annotation></semantics></math>.
It turns out that this optimal linear denoiser for Gaussian captures the limiting behavior of <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math> when <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is large (see <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Denoiser Behavior at Large Noise Levels ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> for a proof).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.Thmtheorem11" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S4.Thmtheorem11.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 4.11</span></span><span id="S4.Thmtheorem11.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S4.Thmtheorem11.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.Thmtheorem11.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.Thmtheorem11.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Assume <math id="S4.Thmtheorem11.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{supp}(p)\subset B_{R}(0)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>supp</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>⊂</mo><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{supp}(p)\subset B_{R}(0)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.Thmtheorem11.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{R}(0)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{R}(0)</annotation></semantics></math> is the open ball of radius <math id="S4.Thmtheorem11.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> centered at the origin.
Then, for any <math id="S4.Thmtheorem11.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta\in(0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta\in(0,1)</annotation></semantics></math> there exists a bounded continuous function
<math id="S4.Thmtheorem11.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S4.Thmtheorem11.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\overline{B_{R}(0)}\times[-\delta,\delta]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\overline{B_{R}(0)}\times[-\delta,\delta]</annotation></semantics></math> such that</span></p>
<table id="S4.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}(x)=m_{\sigma}^{G}(x)+H(x,\sigma)(1+\sigma)^{-2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mi>G</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}(x)=m_{\sigma}^{G}(x)+H(x,\sigma)(1+\sigma)^{-2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">This theorem indicates that for large <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, the denoiser (the one either for the true data distribution <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> or for the empirical distribution over a dataset) is close to being a linear map determined by the mean and covariance of <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>. This validates the empirical observations in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17846v1/publication_figure.svg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/242;" width="452" height="242"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.F4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison of anti-memorization methods.<span id="S4.F4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Training curves showing FID score (solid lines) and memorization ratio (dashed lines) for three methods: 2k-Baseline, 2k-Dummy, and 2k-Gap. Gap training achieves the lowest memorization (0.7%) and best FID (2.35) at final checkpoint.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.3 </span>Medium Noise Regime</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We characterize the medium noise regime by simultaneous transitions in posterior weight concentration and data coverage: as sigma decreases from large to small, posterior weights concentrate on nearest neighbors while data coverage becomes incomplete. The interplay between these two effects creates a volatile training environment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">There are two key observations we have regarding the medium noise regime. The first is the discovery of a <em id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">danger zone</em> for memorization: note that in <a href="#S4.F3" title="In 4.2 Characterization of the Noise Regimes ‣ 4 Geometric Interpretation of Noise Regimes ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> there is a small region of <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> in the medium regime where both coverage and posterior weights are high. In this case, the denoiser <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}^{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}^{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> will tend to learn the empirical optimal <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math> in a region of <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math> is concentrated (due to high Gaussian shell coverage) and furthermore, since this empirical optimal <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math> exhibits high per-noise-level memorization due to the high posterior concentration, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}^{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}^{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> will likely exhibit high per-noise-level memorization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The other observation is that generalization appears to arise primarily in the medium sigma regime. Although we do not yet have a theoretical explanation for this behavior, our empirical results provide strong evidence: swapping denoisers in this regime flips memorization behavior (Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Trajectory-Level memorization. ‣ 3 Empirical Investigation of Memorization ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), with qualitative examples shown in <a href="#A5.F10" title="In E.6 Denoiser Swapping Experiments ‣ Appendix E Experiment Details ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>.
This highlights the medium region as the key regime governing both memorization and generalization in diffusion models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">More theoretical understanding of this regime is left to future work. In the section below, we provide interesting empirical findings regarding this regime: since the medium sigma regime is the most dangerous for memorization, we conjecture that avoiding it during training can mitigate memorization. We validate this idea experimentally in Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Targeted Noise Region Undertraining ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17846v1/figures/danger_zone_combined.png" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/256;" width="405" height="256" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.F5.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
<span id="S4.F5.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Danger zone and gap configurations.</span> The intersection of coverage and max weight curves identifies the danger zone. Memorization rates for different gap configurations are overlaid, showing
that gaps targeting this region minimize memorization.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Targeted Noise Region Undertraining</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our theoretical analysis has identified a “danger zone” in the medium-<math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> regime where memorization risk is highest due to the confluence of high posterior concentration and significant data coverage. A natural question arises: can we mitigate memorization by targeting this specific regime during training? While the swap experiments in <a href="#S3.T1" title="In Trajectory-Level memorization. ‣ 3 Empirical Investigation of Memorization ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> already provides some positive answer, in this section, we further test a rejection training idea on CIFAR-10 and CelebA.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CIFAR-10 car subset.</span>
We consider a CIFAR-10 car subset (2k images) where both generalization and memorization occur <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>. As a baseline, we train standard EDM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> with the full noise schedule <math id="S5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma\in[0.002,80]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0.002</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>80</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma\in[0.002,80]</annotation></semantics></math> (<span id="S5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2k-Baseline</span>). Building on the baseline, we consider two anti-memorization methods: <span id="S5.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2k-Dummy</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite> adds 2k random noise images as a second class to provide distributional contrast; and <span id="S5.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2k-Gap</span> (ours) excludes the danger zone <math id="S5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma\in[1.0,5.0]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>1.0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5.0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma\in[1.0,5.0]</annotation></semantics></math>, identified empirically via coverage and posterior weight analysis (Appendix <a href="#A5.SS4" title="E.4 Danger Zone Identification: 2k Car Subset ‣ Appendix E Experiment Details ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.4</span></a>). We train for 40k iterations, and evaluate at 8 checkpoints. At each checkpoint, we generate 1,024 samples and compute FID against 5k CIFAR-10 training cars and the memorization ratio.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.2.2 Large Noise Regime ‣ 4.2 Characterization of the Noise Regimes ‣ 4 Geometric Interpretation of Noise Regimes ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows training trajectories. The 2k-Baseline exhibits severe memorization (78.8%) with FID 3.72. The 2k-Dummy method substantially reduces memorization to 9.0% with FID 2.58. Our 2k-Gap achieves the best results: 0.7% memorization and FID 2.35.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Grayscale CelebA training data.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, we use downscaled grayscale CelebA data with 1024 training samples, which diffusion models can memorize. We compute the coverage and max weight curves (Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.2.3 Medium Noise Regime ‣ 4.2 Characterization of the Noise Regimes ‣ 4 Geometric Interpretation of Noise Regimes ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>) to identify the danger zone around <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma\in[0.55,1.3]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0.55</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.3</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma\in[0.55,1.3]</annotation></semantics></math> (approximately DDPM timesteps 125–325). We test multiple timestep gap configurations around this region to study the effect on memorization.
We utilize the same DDPM architecture as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> and train for 100k iterations with batch size 512 and the baseline achieves 74.97% memorization.
We then test nine timestep gap configurations, removing different ranges within [100–350] (the danger zone plus some buffer) during training.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Results are summarized in Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.2.3 Medium Noise Regime ‣ 4.2 Characterization of the Noise Regimes ‣ 4 Geometric Interpretation of Noise Regimes ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>. Skipping the full range [100–350] significantly reduces memorization from 75% to 9%. High max weight regions are more influential: the gap [100–200] spanning only 100 timesteps reduces memorization to 43%, while [100–275] achieves 13%.
Visual comparisons of generated samples and their nearest training neighbors are provided in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS5" title="E.5 Pareto Frontier of Training Configurations on 1024 Grayscale CelebA Images ‣ Appendix E Experiment Details ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.5</span></a>, showing high sample quality and meaningful generalization, which validates the memorization mitigation effect. We also include in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS5" title="E.5 Pareto Frontier of Training Configurations on 1024 Grayscale CelebA Images ‣ Appendix E Experiment Details ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.5</span></a> a Pareto frontier analysis over all gap configurations, showing the trade-off between image quality (FID) and memorization; mid-range gaps (150–250, 167–275) achieve the best balance.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Discussion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our results indicate that the trajectory-level memorization in diffusion models arises from a specific medium range of noise levels, rather than from the small or large noise extremes. This per-noise-level analysis provides a fundamentally different perspective for analyzing memorization and generalization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">From a practical perspective, this points to targeted control strategies that act selectively on the intermediate noise regime, such as modifying training emphasis, scheduling, or supervision strength at those scales. More broadly, our framework highlights the importance of incorporating data geometry and noise-scale interactions into the design and analysis of diffusion models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Proof of <a href="#S4.Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 4.2. ‣ 4.1 Key Players for Per-Noise-Level Memorizations ‣ 4 Geometric Interpretation of Noise Regimes ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a></h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">Fix <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta\in(0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta\in(0,1)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q\in(\frac{1}{2},1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q\in(\frac{1}{2},1)</annotation></semantics></math>. Recall that conditioning on <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{X}=x_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝑿</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{X}=x_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> gives <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{X}_{\sigma}:=x_{1}+\sigma\bm{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒁</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{X}_{\sigma}:=x_{1}+\sigma\bm{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{Z}\sim N(0,I_{d})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝒁</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{Z}\sim N(0,I_{d})</annotation></semantics></math>. By definition</span></p>
<table id="A1.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{j}(\bm{X}_{\sigma},\sigma)=\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{\|\bm{X}_{\sigma}-x_{j}\|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)}{\sum_{k=1}^{N}\exp\left(-\frac{\|\bm{X}_{\sigma}-x_{k}\|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{j}(\bm{X}_{\sigma},\sigma)=\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{\|\bm{X}_{\sigma}-x_{j}\|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)}{\sum_{k=1}^{N}\exp\left(-\frac{\|\bm{X}_{\sigma}-x_{k}\|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">For ease of notation write <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{j}=w_{j}(\bm{X}_{\sigma},\sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{j}=w_{j}(\bm{X}_{\sigma},\sigma)</annotation></semantics></math> and notice that since <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j}=1</annotation></semantics></math> we have</span></p>

<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text">Let <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{d}_{j}:=x_{j}-x_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{d}_{j}:=x_{j}-x_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{j}\in\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{j}\in\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>. By direct calculation we have</span></p>

<p id="A1.SS1.p2.8" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.8.1" class="ltx_text">For any fixed <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j\neq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j\neq 1</annotation></semantics></math>, the key idea is to observe that <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\langle\bm{Z},\hat{d}_{j}\rangle\sim N(0,\|\hat{d}_{j}\|^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mi>𝒁</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\langle\bm{Z},\hat{d}_{j}\rangle\sim N(0,\|\hat{d}_{j}\|^{2})</annotation></semantics></math>. <p id="A1.SS1.p2.9" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.9.1" class="ltx_text">where <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> is the CDF of the standard normal distribution. Put <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z:=F^{-1}(\delta/K)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z:=F^{-1}(\delta/K)</annotation></semantics></math> and note that since <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> are increasing functions we may write</span></p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E12.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\frac{\|\hat{d}_{j}\|}{2\sigma}+\frac{\sigma c_{K}}{\|\hat{d}_{j}\|}\leq z\quad\iff\quad F\Big(\frac{\|\hat{d}_{j}\|}{2\sigma}+\frac{\sigma c_{K}}{\|\hat{d}_{j}\|}\Big)\leq\frac{\delta}{K}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>≤</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mfrac><mi>δ</mi><mi>K</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\|\hat{d}_{j}\|}{2\sigma}+\frac{\sigma c_{K}}{\|\hat{d}_{j}\|}\leq z\quad\iff\quad F\Big(\frac{\|\hat{d}_{j}\|}{2\sigma}+\frac{\sigma c_{K}}{\|\hat{d}_{j}\|}\Big)\leq\frac{\delta}{K}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(12)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.10" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.10.1" class="ltx_text">Solving the equation</span></p>

<p id="A1.SS1.p2.11" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.11.1" class="ltx_text">yields a positive solution</span></p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{K,\delta,q}:=z+\sqrt{z^{2}-2c_{K}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{K,\delta,q}:=z+\sqrt{z^{2}-2c_{K}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<p id="A1.SS1.p2.12" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.12.1" class="ltx_text">which is well defined since <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{K}&lt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{K}&lt;0</annotation></semantics></math>. Calculus shows that the function <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g(a)=\frac{a}{2}+\frac{c_{K}}{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mi>a</mi></mfrac></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g(a)=\frac{a}{2}+\frac{c_{K}}{a}</annotation></semantics></math> is increasing for all <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, hence for all <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>
<table id="A1.E13" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\|\hat{d}_{j}\|}{\sigma}\leq a_{K,\delta,q}\quad\implies\quad\frac{\|\hat{d}_{j}\|}{2\sigma}+\frac{\sigma c_{K}}{\|\hat{d}_{j}\|}\leq z." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>σ</mi></mfrac><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mo stretchy="false">⟹</mo><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\|\hat{d}_{j}\|}{\sigma}\leq a_{K,\delta,q}\quad\implies\quad\frac{\|\hat{d}_{j}\|}{2\sigma}+\frac{\sigma c_{K}}{\|\hat{d}_{j}\|}\leq z.</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<p id="A1.SS1.p2.13" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.13.1" class="ltx_text">Thus by <a href="#A1.E12" title="In Proof. ‣ A.1 Proof of ‣ Appendix A Posterior Concentration and Cosine Similarity Concentration ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eqn.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> and <a href="#A1.E13" title="In Proof. ‣ A.1 Proof of ‣ Appendix A Posterior Concentration and Cosine Similarity Concentration ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eqn.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> we have the following implication:
<br class="ltx_break">If</span></p>

<p id="A1.SS1.p2.15" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.15.1" class="ltx_text">for all <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j\in\{2,\dots,K+1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j\in\{2,\dots,K+1\}</annotation></semantics></math>. By <a href="#A1.E10" title="In Proof. ‣ A.1 Proof of ‣ Appendix A Posterior Concentration and Cosine Similarity Concentration ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eqn.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> and <a href="#A1.E11" title="In Proof. ‣ A.1 Proof of ‣ Appendix A Posterior Concentration and Cosine Similarity Concentration ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eqn.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> this further implies</span></p>

<p id="A1.SS1.p2.17" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.17.1" class="ltx_text">implies for <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m31" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K_{*}:=\arg\min_{K}(d_{K}/a_{K,\delta,q})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><msub><mi>min</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K_{*}:=\arg\min_{K}(d_{K}/a_{K,\delta,q})</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>

<p id="A1.SS1.p2.18" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.18.1" class="ltx_text">and on <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m32" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}_{K_{*}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}_{K_{*}}</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>

<p id="A1.SS1.p2.19" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.19.1" class="ltx_text">Plugging in the respective definitions for <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m33" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{K}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m34" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> into <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m35" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{K,\delta,q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{K,\delta,q}</annotation></semantics></math> completes the proof of the first implication. 
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">To prove the second implication, let</span></p>
<table id="A1.Ex22" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex22.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c:=\log\left(\frac{1-q}{q(N-1)}\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c:=\log\left(\frac{1-q}{q(N-1)}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>

<p id="A1.SS1.p2.20" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.20.1" class="ltx_text">and notice that <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m36" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c&lt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c&lt;0</annotation></semantics></math>. <p id="A1.SS1.p2.28" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.28.1" class="ltx_text">Since <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m47" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{1}\leq\|\hat{d}_{j}\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{1}\leq\|\hat{d}_{j}\|</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m48" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>, by <a href="#A1.E16" title="In Proof. ‣ A.1 Proof of ‣ Appendix A Posterior Concentration and Cosine Similarity Concentration ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eqn.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a> and <a href="#A1.E17" title="In Proof. ‣ A.1 Proof of ‣ Appendix A Posterior Concentration and Cosine Similarity Concentration ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eqn.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> we have the following implication:
<br class="ltx_break">If</span></p>

<p id="A1.SS1.p2.30" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.30.1" class="ltx_text">for all <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m49" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j\neq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j\neq 1</annotation></semantics></math>. By the above union bound in <a href="#A1.E14" title="In Proof. ‣ A.1 Proof of ‣ Appendix A Posterior Concentration and Cosine Similarity Concentration ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eqn.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> and <a href="#A1.E15" title="In Proof. ‣ A.1 Proof of ‣ Appendix A Posterior Concentration and Cosine Similarity Concentration ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eqn.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> this further implies</span></p>

<p id="A1.SS1.p2.32" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.32.1" class="ltx_text">which implies that <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m51" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma\leq\frac{d_{1}}{b_{\delta,q}}=\frac{d_{2NN}(x_{1})}{b_{\delta,q}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>≤</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma\leq\frac{d_{1}}{b_{\delta,q}}=\frac{d_{2NN}(x_{1})}{b_{\delta,q}}</annotation></semantics></math> yields the same implication. This completes the proof.
∎</span></p>

</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Cosine Similarity Concentration</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The following lemma is similar to <a href="#S4.Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 4.2. ‣ 4.1 Key Players for Per-Noise-Level Memorizations ‣ 4 Geometric Interpretation of Noise Regimes ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a> with an additional bound on the distance from the denoiser <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{\sigma}(\bm{X}_{\sigma})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{\sigma}(\bm{X}_{\sigma})</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> given that <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{X}_{\sigma}=x_{1}+\sigma\bm{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒁</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{X}_{\sigma}=x_{1}+\sigma\bm{Z}</annotation></semantics></math>. This demonstrates that for small <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> the empirical optimal denoiser admits nearest neighbor behavior. Furthermore this result leads to <a href="#A1.Thmtheorem2" title="Corollary A.2. ‣ A.2 Cosine Similarity Concentration ‣ Appendix A Posterior Concentration and Cosine Similarity Concentration ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Corollary</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a>, where following inspiration from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>, we demonstrate a conditional bound on the cosine similarity between the optimal and conditional vector fields in the flow matching setting with linear schedules.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lemma">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma A.1</span></span><span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{N}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo>⊂</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{N}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> be a finite data set with uniform distribution <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\mathcal{D}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\mathcal{D}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Define</span></p>
<table id="A1.Ex32" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex32.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D:=\max_{1\leq i,j\leq N}\|x_{i}-x_{j}\|." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>:=</mo><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></mrow></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D:=\max_{1\leq i,j\leq N}\|x_{i}-x_{j}\|.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">let <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{d}_{j}:=x_{j}-x_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{d}_{j}:=x_{j}-x_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Fix <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> and condition on <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{X}=x_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐗</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{X}=x_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, then with probability at least <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\delta</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>
<table id="A1.Ex33" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex33.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{1}(\bm{X}_{\sigma},\sigma)\geq 1-\epsilon" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{1}(\bm{X}_{\sigma},\sigma)\geq 1-\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">and consequently</span></p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E18.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|m_{\sigma}(\bm{X}_{\sigma})-x_{1}\|\leq D\left(1-w_{1}(\bm{X}_{\sigma},\sigma)\right)\leq D\epsilon" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|m_{\sigma}(\bm{X}_{\sigma})-x_{1}\|\leq D\left(1-w_{1}(\bm{X}_{\sigma},\sigma)\right)\leq D\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(18)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where</span></p>
<table id="A1.Ex34" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<div id="A1.SS2.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">Let <math id="A1.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> and recall that <math id="A1.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{X}=x_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝑿</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{X}=x_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> gives <math id="A1.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{X}_{\sigma}=x_{1}+\sigma\bm{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒁</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{X}_{\sigma}=x_{1}+\sigma\bm{Z}</annotation></semantics></math>. We have</span></p>

Since <math id="A1.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j}=1</annotation></semantics></math> we have</span></p>

<p id="A1.SS2.p2.8" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.p2.8.1" class="ltx_text">which gives <math id="A1.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{1}\geq 1-\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{1}\geq 1-\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> by <a href="#A1.E19" title="In Proof. ‣ A.2 Cosine Similarity Concentration ‣ Appendix A Posterior Concentration and Cosine Similarity Concentration ‣ Two Calm Ends and the Wild Middle:A Geometric Picture of Memorization in Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eqn.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>. Since <math id="A1.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\langle\bm{Z},\hat{d}_{j}\right\rangle\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\|\hat{d}_{j}\|^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>⟨</mo><mrow><mi>𝒁</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>⟩</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\langle\bm{Z},\hat{d}_{j}\right\rangle\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\|\hat{d}_{j}\|^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> we have by union bound</span></p>
<table id="A1.Ex42" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex42.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}^{c})\leq\sum_{j\neq 1}\mathbb{P}\left(\left\langle\bm{Z},\frac{\hat{d}_{j}}{\|\hat{d}_{j}\|}\right\rangle&gt;\frac{\|\hat{d}_{j}\|}{2\sigma}+\frac{\sigma\kappa_{\epsilon}}{\|\hat{d}_{j}\|}\right)=\sum_{j\neq
